title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design (CaMeL)
finding: CaMeL extracts control and data flow from the trusted query so untrusted data can never change program flow, and uses capabilities to enforce policies at tool-call time; per authors it solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security vs 84% undefended.
why_for_us: Template for our CRM/email/payment agents: planner sees only the user task, quarantined LLM parses untrusted content into typed values, policy engine checks capabilities before any send/pay tool call.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
finding: Extensible environment with 97 realistic tasks (email client, e-banking, travel) and 629 security test cases (per authors, preprint abstract W7128378279); SOTA LLMs fail many tasks even without attacks, and existing attacks break some but not all security properties.
why_for_us: Run AgentDojo (banking + workspace suites) against our vLLM Qwen3 agents to get a baseline utility/ASR before and after adding any defense.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
finding: 1,054 test cases over 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools, 30 agents evaluated; per authors ReAct-prompted GPT-4 was vulnerable 24% of the time and a reinforcing hacking prompt nearly doubled the ASR.
why_for_us: Cheap, text-only benchmark to regression-test every new open-weight model version we deploy (attack categories include data exfiltration, directly relevant to PESEL/AML data).

title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
finding: Per authors, all eight evaluated IPI defenses were bypassed by adaptive attacks, consistently with attack success rate over 50%.
why_for_us: Do not rely on detector/filter-style defenses (prompt guards, classifiers) as the security boundary for payment or email tools; treat them as telemetry only.

title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
finding: Using tuned gradient descent, RL, random search and human red-teaming, authors bypass 12 recent defenses with ASR above 90% for most, although most originally reported near-zero ASR.
why_for_us: Any vendor claim of near-zero ASR for a guardrail product should be discounted; our acceptance tests must include adaptive (iterated) attacks, not static strings.

title: Defending Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks With Spotlighting
finding: Spotlighting (delimiting, datamarking, encoding untrusted input to signal provenance) reduced ASR from greater than 50% to below 2% on GPT-family models with minimal task impact, per authors (static attacks).
why_for_us: Zero-cost hygiene layer for emails/documents fed to agents (datamark or base64-encode untrusted blocks), but per S004/S005 never the only control.

title: The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions
finding: Argues a root cause of injections is that LLMs treat system prompts and untrusted third-party text with equal priority, and proposes training an explicit instruction hierarchy.
why_for_us: When choosing open models (Qwen3.x etc.) prefer ones trained with role/priority separation and always put tool output in tool role, never concatenated into the user turn.

title: SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization
finding: Preference optimization on (injected input, secure output, insecure output) triples; per authors it is the first method reducing success of various injections to below 10%, including stronger unseen attacks, with similar utility.
why_for_us: Recipe we could replicate on our own GPU (DPO on a 14B model with synthetic injected CRM/email samples) and then measure with AgentDojo, accepting S005 caveat.

title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
finding: Separates prompt and data into structured channels with special delimiters and fine-tunes the model to only follow instructions in the prompt channel.
why_for_us: Supports designing our tool APIs so that data fields are never interpreted as instructions (separate channels), useful baseline vs SecAlign.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
finding: Proposes principled design patterns giving agents provable resistance to prompt injection and analyses their utility/security trade-offs with case studies.
why_for_us: Checklist for architecture review of each agent (which pattern applies: plan-then-execute, dual LLM, action selector, context minimization) before giving it payment/email tools.

title: DRIFT: Dynamic Rule-Based Defense with Injection Isolation for Securing LLM Agents
finding: Secure planner builds minimal function trajectory plus JSON-schema parameter checklist; dynamic validator checks deviations; injection isolator masks conflicting instructions in memory; strong security with high utility on AgentDojo, ASB, AgentDyn (per authors, no numbers in abstract).
why_for_us: Practical middle ground between CaMeL and nothing: per-task allowlist of functions plus argument schema, validated outside the model.

title: IPIGuard: A Novel Tool Dependency Graph-Based Defense Against Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
finding: Models agent execution as a pre-planned tool dependency graph so tool responses cannot add new tool invocations.
why_for_us: Simple enforceable rule for our harness: tool calls not in the pre-approved plan graph require human confirmation.

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning on Real-World MCP Servers
finding: 45 live MCP servers, 353 tools, 1,348 malicious cases; per authors o1-mini reached 72.8% ASR, more capable models were often more susceptible, and the highest refusal rate (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) was below 3%.
why_for_us: Pin and hash every MCP tool description we load (CRM, email, payments) and diff on change; never auto-load third-party MCP servers into agents that also hold payment tools.

title: When MCP Servers Attack: Taxonomy, Feasibility, and Mitigation
finding: Component-based taxonomy of 12 attack categories for malicious MCP servers with PoCs across real host-LLM settings; malicious servers can be generated at virtually no cost and state-of-the-art scanners were insufficient (per authors).
why_for_us: Treat MCP servers as untrusted code: run them in separate containers with no secrets beyond their own scope, and do not trust a scanner pass as approval.

title: Beyond Tool Poisoning: Attack Surfaces of Malicious Remote MCP Servers Across LLM Platforms
finding: Evaluated on ChatGPT, Claude Desktop and Gemini CLI; host-side filtering varied sharply (95% vs 50% ASR on the same email request), description and response channels succeeded on disjoint scenarios, and successful attacks were almost never disclosed to the user (per authors).
why_for_us: Log and surface raw MCP request/response payloads to the human reviewer; the agent's own summary will not reveal a compromise.

title: Skill-Inject: Measuring Agent Vulnerability to Skill File Attacks
finding: 202 injection-task pairs hidden in agent skill files; per authors frontier agents reach up to 80% ASR, executing data exfiltration, destructive and ransomware-like actions; scaling or simple input filtering unlikely to fix it.
why_for_us: Our Claude Code / harness skills and plugin files must be code-reviewed and pinned like dependencies (CODEOWNERS on .claude/ and skills dirs), never pulled from open registries unreviewed.

title: ETDI: Mitigating Tool Squatting and Rug Pull Attacks in MCP by Using OAuth-Enhanced Tool Definitions and Policy-Based Access Control
finding: Security extension to MCP with cryptographic identity verification, immutable versioned tool definitions and policy-based access control against tool poisoning and rug pulls.
why_for_us: Concrete design for our internal MCP servers: signed, versioned tool manifests; client refuses silently changed definitions (rug pull).

title: MCP Safety Audit: LLMs with the Model Context Protocol Allow Major Security Exploits
finding: Early audit showing that connecting LLMs to standard MCP servers enables major exploits (title claim; abstract in OpenAlex truncated, no numbers available).
why_for_us: Use as a test-idea source for red-teaming our filesystem/DB MCP servers in the lab sandbox.

title: Progent: Securing AI Agents with Privilege Control
finding: Symbolic policy over tool names and arguments checked deterministically on every call; LLM drafts the policy, an SMT solver classifies updates as narrowing (auto) or expansion (needs approval), giving monotonic confinement; significantly reduces ASR on AgentDojo and ASB while keeping utility (per authors).
why_for_us: Directly implementable in our harness: per-task policy file (e.g. email.send only to domain X, payments.create max amount Y) enforced outside the model, expansions require human approval in GitHub.

title: MiniScope: Authorizing Agents with Least-Privilege Permissions
finding: Task-centric hierarchical permission model; per authors reduces simulated permission confirmations by 43.4%-89.4% vs per-tool prompting, mitigates all privilege-escalation attacks tested, and found six overprivileged connector configurations in ChatGPT and Claude.
why_for_us: Addresses approval fatigue for our human reviewer: group permissions by task role instead of approving each tool call.

title: Capability Gates Are Not Authorization: Confused-Deputy Failures in LLM Agent Frameworks
finding: LangChain/LangGraph, LlamaIndex and Stripe Agent Toolkit gate tool exposure but none re-authorizes each call with concrete argument values by default; an unauthorized payout executes under LangChain default dispatch; proposed ScopeGate PDP/PEP (scope, authorization, money ceiling, idempotency, default deny) showed 0/48 static bypasses and 0/29 adaptive unauthorized attempts (per author).
why_for_us: Exactly our payments risk: add a fail-closed per-call authorization gate with money ceiling and idempotency key in front of every payment/transfer tool, independent of the agent framework.

title: Evaluating Privilege Usage of Agents with Real-World Tools (GrantBox)
finding: Sandbox integrating real-world tools with genuine privileges; LLMs block some direct attacks but average ASR was 84.80% in carefully crafted scenarios (per authors).
why_for_us: Argues for testing agents against real (sandboxed) tool privileges rather than mocked tools; mirror our CRM/email tools into a lab copy for red-teaming.

title: What Breaks When LLMs Code? Characterizing Operational Safety Failures of Agentic Code Assistants
finding: From 16,586 GitHub issues of coding tools, 547 confirmed safety failures, 326 rated high/critical; dominant risks are constraint violations, destructive operations, authorization bypasses and deception; over 65% arise in bug fixing and setup/configuration (per authors).
why_for_us: Our main risk is benign-task failures, not attackers: enforce read-only mounts for anything outside the task dir, block destructive git/db commands in the container, and verify success claims by CI rather than agent reports.

title: Beyond Static Sandboxing: Learned Capability Governance for Autonomous AI Agents
finding: Identifies capability overprovisioning: open agent runtimes expose every tool to every session, a 15x overprovision ratio for summarization vs deployment tasks (per authors); proposes per-session tool scoping learned from audit logs.
why_for_us: Cheap win: task cards should declare the tool set and the harness should only expose those tools (no shell for summarization tasks).

title: APPA: Recoverable Information-Flow Control for Real-World LLM Agents
finding: Notes that monotone taint tracking in IFC either over-blocks or strands execution once an agent reads unvetted data, and proposes recoverable IFC for agent permissions.
why_for_us: Relevant if we adopt taint-based gating (S001/S019): plan for a declassification/review step so agents are not permanently blocked after reading an email.

title: Vulnerability Detection with Code Language Models: How Far are We? (PrimeVul)
finding: Existing vuln datasets have poor labels and duplication; a SOTA 7B model scored 68.26% F1 on BigVul but only 3.09% F1 on PrimeVul, and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 were akin to random guessing in the strictest setting (per authors).
why_for_us: Do not use a function-level LLM classifier as our security gate; use LLMs for triage/explanation on top of SAST and tests, and evaluate on deduplicated, time-split data.

title: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
finding: 89 CWE Top-25 scenarios produced 1,689 programs, of which approximately 40% were vulnerable (per authors).
why_for_us: Foundational baseline justifying mandatory CodeQL/Semgrep on every agent PR; compare our Qwen agents' rate on the same scenario set.

title: CVE-Bench: A Benchmark for AI Agents' Ability to Exploit Real-World Web Application Vulnerabilities
finding: Sandbox of critical-severity web-app CVEs; per authors the state-of-the-art agent framework exploited up to 13% of vulnerabilities.
why_for_us: Calibrates threat: autonomous web exploitation is real but still low-rate; also a ready harness to pentest a staging copy of our SaaS with our own agents.

title: Cybench: A Framework for Evaluating Cybersecurity Capabilities and Risks of Language Models
finding: 40 professional CTF tasks with subtasks; without guidance, top agents solved complete tasks that took human teams up to 11 minutes, while the hardest took humans 24h54m (per authors).
why_for_us: Use as a capability yardstick for our open models before using them for internal security review tasks.

title: ATLANTIS: AI-driven Threat Localization, Analysis, and Triage Intelligence System
finding: Winning cyber reasoning system of DARPA AIxCC finals (DEF CON 33, Aug 2025); combines LLMs with symbolic execution, directed fuzzing and static analysis for discovery and patching; artifacts released.
why_for_us: Lesson: winning systems pair LLMs with classic program analysis; our security agent should orchestrate fuzzers/SAST, not replace them.

title: Fuzz4All: Universal Fuzzing with Large Language Models
finding: LLM as input generator/mutator with autoprompting across 6 input languages; higher coverage than language-specific fuzzers and 98 bugs found, 64 confirmed previously unknown (per authors).
why_for_us: Pattern for fuzzing our own parsers (KW/EKW XML, KRZ notices, bank statement imports) with LLM-generated structured inputs on idle GPU time.

title: How Effective Are They? Exploring Large Language Model Based Fuzz Driver Generation
finding: Systematic study of LLM-generated fuzz drivers for library API fuzzing (abstract in OpenAlex truncated; no numbers extracted).
why_for_us: Reference for an agent task card: generate fuzz harnesses for our TypeScript/Python parsing libraries and keep only those that compile and add coverage.

title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
finding: Models trained to write secure code when the year is 2023 but insert exploitable code for 2024 kept the backdoor through SFT, RL and adversarial training; adversarial training could teach models to hide triggers better (per authors).
why_for_us: Open-weight coding models from unknown fine-tuners are a real risk: use only official base/instruct weights with verified hashes and keep SAST on every agent PR regardless of model.

title: Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples
finding: Pretraining 600M-13B models, 250 poisoned documents compromised models across all sizes despite 20x more clean data for the largest; same dynamics shown for fine-tuning (per authors).
why_for_us: If we fine-tune on scraped or user-submitted text (emails, notary docs), a few hundred malicious samples suffice: require provenance and filtering for every fine-tuning sample.

title: Models Are Codes: Towards Measuring Malicious Code Poisoning Attacks on Pre-trained Model Hubs (MalHug)
finding: Deployed at Ant Group on a Hugging Face mirror for 3+ months, monitoring 705K models and 176K datasets, finding 91 malicious models and 9 malicious dataset loading scripts (reverse shells, credential theft, recon) (per authors).
why_for_us: On rented GPUs load only safetensors, set trust_remote_code=False, and never run dataset loading scripts; pre-download and hash models outside the GPU node.

title: ShadowPickle: Evading Machine Learning Model Scanners via Stealthy Pickle Deserialization Attacks
finding: Three stealthy pickle attacks evade ten SOTA scanners and four model hubs; the Overwritten variant has a 63% evasion rate across scanners (per authors).
why_for_us: Scanner pass is not safety: ban pickle-format weights (.bin/.pt) entirely in our pipeline.

title: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
finding: Describes real attacks (model replaced by malware, trained on vulnerable framework or poisoned data) and how Sigstore can let publishers sign models and prove dataset properties.
why_for_us: Sign our own fine-tuned LoRA adapters/models (Sigstore model signing) and verify signatures before vLLM loads them; supports DORA ICT supply-chain evidence.

title: TrojanPuzzle: Covertly Poisoning Code-Suggestion Models
finding: Covert and TrojanPuzzle plant poison in out-of-context regions such as docstrings and never include the full payload, evading static analysis and signature-based dataset cleansing.
why_for_us: If we fine-tune coding models on our repos plus external code, docstrings/comments are an attack channel; restrict training data to reviewed internal code.

title: Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models
finding: Black-box attacks on GPT-2 fine-tuned on case law, health and email data extract up to 10x more PII than prior attacks; scrubbing reduces but does not prevent leakage and sentence-level DP still leaks about 3% of PII sequences (per authors).
why_for_us: Before fine-tuning on notary/loan documents: pseudonymize PESEL/names/addresses at source, and treat DP as risk reduction not GDPR anonymization.

title: Pandora's White-Box: Precise Training Data Detection and Extraction in Large Language Models
finding: A simple loss-ratio attack between base and fine-tuned model gives near-perfect membership inference, and over 50% of the fine-tuning dataset could be extracted from fine-tuned Pythia and Llama models (per authors).
why_for_us: Anyone who obtains our fine-tuned weights plus the public base model can likely recover much of the training set; adapters trained on personal data must be handled as personal data (access control, DPIA).

title: LoRA-Leak: Membership Inference Attacks Against LoRA Fine-tuned Language Models
finding: 15 MIAs (5 using the pre-trained model as reference) show LoRA fine-tuned LMs remain vulnerable (e.g. 0.775 AUC under conservative settings); of four defenses only dropout and excluding specific layers mitigated risk while keeping utility (per authors).
why_for_us: Run LoRA-Leak against our own adapters as a release gate; add dropout and layer exclusion to our LoRA recipe.

title: Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models
finding: Gigabytes of training data extracted from open and closed models; a divergence attack made aligned ChatGPT emit training data at a 150x higher rate; alignment does not remove memorization (per authors).
why_for_us: Alignment or system prompts are not a privacy control for models trained on our data; output filtering for PII patterns is still needed.

title: SoK: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs are Rushing Nowhere (and How to Fix It)
finding: Many recent LLM MIA methods are evaluated on post-hoc collected member/non-member sets, which confounds results.
why_for_us: When we audit our models, build member/non-member sets by random held-out split from the same distribution, otherwise results are meaningless.

title: Your Code Secret Belongs to Me: Neural Code Completion Tools Can Memorize Hard-Coded Credentials
finding: HCR tool shows commercial and open code completion tools emit memorized training data and extra secret strings; two valid credentials were found (per authors).
why_for_us: Never fine-tune on repos or agent logs containing secrets; run gitleaks/trufflehog on agent trajectories and training corpora before use.

title: Evaluating the Security Posture of Real-World FIDO2 Deployments
finding: FIDO2 security guarantees assume benign client-side components; the paper evaluates real deployments under that assumption (abstract in OpenAlex is short, no numbers).
why_for_us: When adding passkeys for investors/notaries, keep server-side checks strict (origin, rpId, user verification flag, signature counter) and do not trust client-reported state.

title: Passkeys in Practice: An Empirical Evaluation of FIDO2/WebAuthn Compliance and Interoperability
finding: Empirical study of passkey implementations across browsers and devices, motivated by untested real-world interoperability.
why_for_us: Plan a fallback/recovery path and a cross-browser test matrix before making passkeys primary auth in the notary SaaS.

title: Detecting Broken Object-Level Authorization Vulnerabilities in Database-Backed Applications
finding: Study of 101 real-world BOLA vulnerabilities in open-source apps identifying the four most common object-level authorization models (per authors).
why_for_us: BOLA (IDOR) is the top risk for our client/loan endpoints; generate per-endpoint cross-tenant access tests with agents, using these authorization models as the checklist.

title: RLS Side Channels: Investigating Leakage of Row-Level Security Protected Data Through Query Execution Time
venue: Proc. ACM on Management of Data (SIGMOD)
finding: In PostgreSQL and SQL Server an attacker can craft index-using queries whose timing reveals whether an unauthorized value exists in an RLS-protected table, demonstrated against managed AWS instances; a data-oblivious scheme for unique keys mitigates it (per authors).
why_for_us: Our Supabase RLS stops direct reads but not timing oracles: do not expose arbitrary filter/query capability (e.g. PostgREST filters on sensitive columns like PESEL) to tenants or agents.

title: CORTEX: Collaborative LLM Agents for High-Stakes Alert Triage
finding: Multi-agent triage (behavior analysis, evidence gathering, reasoning agent) over real evidence reduces false positives vs single-agent LLMs; releases a dataset of production SOC investigations (no numbers in abstract).
why_for_us: Pattern for a small-team SOC-lite: agent gathers Supabase/Cloudflare log evidence and drafts an auditable verdict for AML/fraud alerts, human decides.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Log Analysis, Security, and Interpretation
venue: Journal of Network and Systems Management
finding: Benchmarks fine-tuned BERT-family and GPT-2/GPT-Neo models for security log classification (no abstract in OpenAlex; numbers not extracted).
why_for_us: Suggests small fine-tuned encoders may suffice for log classification on our own GPU instead of large generative models.

title: We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs
finding: 16 code LLMs, 576,000 samples: average hallucinated packages at least 5.2% for commercial and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique hallucinated names (per authors).
why_for_us: Our open-weight agents will invent packages: block network installs in the container and require any new dependency to pass an allowlist/registry-age check in CI before merge.

title: The Early Bird Catches the Leak: Unveiling Timing Side Channels in LLM Serving Systems
finding: Shared KV cache and semantic cache create timing side channels that let an adversary infer system prompts and other users' prompts token-by-token; shown feasible against popular online services (per authors).
why_for_us: If we ever serve one vLLM instance to several clients/tenants, disable cross-tenant prefix caching or partition it per tenant.

title: Auditing Prompt Caching in Language Model APIs
finding: Statistical timing audits detected global cache sharing across users in seven API providers, including OpenAI, implying potential prompt leakage (per authors).
why_for_us: Check provider cache scope (org vs global) before sending client PII in prompts; prefer providers with org-scoped caching for DORA/GDPR.

title: LeftoverLocals: Listening to LLM Responses Through Leaked GPU Local Memory
finding: GPU local memory from another process is recoverable on Apple, Qualcomm and AMD GPUs; PoC listens to another user's llama.cpp session across process/container boundaries (per authors).
why_for_us: NVIDIA is not in the affected list in the abstract, but the class of risk applies to shared rented GPUs: never put production PII through community-cloud GPUs (SaladCloud nodes are third-party machines).

title: GPUHammer: Rowhammer Attacks on GPU Memories are Practical
finding: First Rowhammer on a discrete NVIDIA GPU (A6000, GDDR6): up to 8 bit-flips across 4 banks, enough to tamper with ML models causing accuracy drops up to 80% (per authors).
why_for_us: Low priority for us, but on shared GPUs verify model output checksums/eval canaries after long runs; RTX 5090 (GDDR7) not covered by the paper, so status unknown.

title: Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!
finding: GPT-3.5 Turbo guardrails were jailbroken by fine-tuning on only 10 adversarial examples for under $0.20 via the API, and benign fine-tuning datasets also degraded safety alignment (per authors).
why_for_us: After every fine-tune of our agents (even on benign data), rerun safety and prompt-injection evals before deployment; alignment of the base model does not carry over automatically.

title: Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment
finding: Fine-tuning on narrowly harmful datasets can make models broadly misaligned (emergent misalignment, unexpected per an expert survey); authors build improved model organisms reaching 99% coherence.
why_for_us: Never fine-tune agents on raw trajectories that include insecure or reward-hacked code; filter training data with SAST and reviewer verdicts first.

title: Beyond Prompt Injection: The Tool Update Gap in LLM Agent Security
finding: ETUDE wstawia złośliwe działanie w aktualizację początkowo niegroźnego narzędzia; kod działa poza kontekstem modelu, więc omija obrony oparte na treści widocznej dla modelu. Według autorów 97,6% skuteczności ataku przy 95,9% poprawnie wykonanych zadań, w 7 frameworkach, w tym Gemini CLI, Codex CLI i Claude Code.
why_for_us: Przypinać wersje (lockfile + skrót) serwerów MCP i paczek narzędzi agentów; aktualizacja narzędzia = przegląd jak zmiana kodu, nie automat.

title: Pinned, but Blind in the Schema: The Benign-Change Cost and Nested-Text Blind Spot of MCP Tool Pinning
finding: Na 2040 parach wersji narzędzi: przypięcie całego rekordu oflagowało 100% niegroźnych zmian; przypięcie samego opisu wykryło 40% złośliwych i 0% trucizny w zagnieżdżonym schemacie, nowych parametrach i wartościach domyślnych; skaner wzorców miał recall 0 na parafrazach (według autorów).
why_for_us: Przypinać cały rekord narzędzia (opis + schemat + wartości domyślne), a zmiany przeglądać warstwowo; nie polegać na skanerze słów kluczowych.

title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
finding: Proces współdzielący GPU, mierząc czas własnych kerneli, odgadł ustawienie zatwierdzania akcji agenta (pytaj/nie pytaj) z dokładnością zbalansowaną 94,17% na rzadkim modelu MoE w trybie eager (według autorów).
why_for_us: Na współdzielonych węzłach (Salad) zakładać, że sąsiad widzi wzorzec pracy GPU; nic poufnego nie powinno zależeć od tajności promptu ani konfiguracji agenta.

title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation
finding: Różnica czasu do pierwszego tokenu między trafieniem a chybieniem w pamięci KV pozwala odgadywać cudze fragmenty promptów przy współdzielonym prefix cache; Mirage opóźnia emisję na bramie zamiast wyłączać współdzielenie.
why_for_us: Jeśli kiedyś jeden serwer vLLM obsłuży kilku najemców (NotarAI / Finance You / klienci), prefix cache nie może być współdzielony między nimi bez takiej ochrony.

title: The More You Tune, the More They Spill? An empirical study of data leakage from code models under fine-tuning, quantization, and parameter-efficient adaptation
finding: Na StarCoder2 dostrajanie obniża wydobywalność danych pretreningu z 54,9% do 23,5%, ale zwiększa podatność danych dostrajania, zwłaszcza w małych modelach; int4 wzmacnia względny wyciek danych dostrajania; PEFT ogranicza zapamiętywanie w porównaniu z pełnym dostrajaniem (według autorów).
why_for_us: Dostrajać przez LoRA, nie pełne dostrajanie; po kwantyzacji int4 powtórzyć test wycieku; do danych treningowych tylko pseudonimizowane kody i trajektorie.
